trial_name: CAAM — Effect of Bag-Mask Ventilation vs Endotracheal Intubation During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation on Neurological Outcome After Out-of-Hospital Cardiorespiratory Arrest (2018)
citation: Jabre P, Penaloza A, Pinero D, et al. Effect of Bag-Mask Ventilation vs Endotracheal Intubation During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation on Neurologic Outcome After Out-of-Hospital Cardiorespiratory Arrest: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018;319(8):779-787
one_liner: In adults with non-shockable OHCA, initial bag-mask ventilation did not meet non-inferiority vs endotracheal intubation for 28-day favourable neurological outcome, with similar survival but differing safety profiles.

pico.population: Adults (≥18 years) with non-traumatic OHCA and initial non-shockable rhythm, treated by physician-led prehospital ALS teams
pico.intervention: Initial bag-mask ventilation (BMV) by emergency physician; rescue intubation permitted for failure/regurgitation
pico.comparison: Initial endotracheal intubation (ETI) by emergency physician; rescue BMV permitted before/between attempts or if failure
pico.outcome: Favourable neurological outcome at 28 days (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2)

background.existing_knowledge: Airway strategies during OHCA lacked high-quality comparative evidence. ETI offers a definitive airway but may cause interruptions and misplacement; BMV is immediately deployable but risks gastric insufflation and inadequate ventilation. Prior evidence was observational and confounded.
background.knowledge_gap: No randomised evidence comparing initial BMV vs ETI strategies in OHCA existed.
background.hypothesis: In adults with non-traumatic OHCA and initial non-shockable rhythm, initial BMV is non-inferior to initial ETI for 28-day favourable neurological outcome (non-inferiority margin: 1.0% absolute difference).

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, open-label, parallel-group, non-inferiority trial; stratified by centre with permuted blocks; prehospital physician-led advanced life support.
methods.setting: 15 centres in France and 5 centres in Belgium, basic life support teams plus physician-staffed ALS units.

inclusion: no spontaneous breathing and requiring advanced airway management

methods.intervention: Initial BMV by emergency physician. Rescue intubation allowed for ventilation failure or regurgitation.
methods.comparison: Initial ETI by emergency physician during CPR. Rescue BMV allowed before/between intubation attempts and in case of failure.
methods.blinding: Open-label; 28-day neurological outcome assessed by a blinded investigator.
methods.sample_size_power: Assuming 3.0% favourable neurological outcome in both groups, 2000 patients needed for 80% power at 1-sided α=2.5% with 1.0% absolute non-inferiority margin. Primary analysis ITT with supportive per-protocol and modified ITT analyses.

headline_bullets: Favourable neurological outcome was similarly low in both groups (4.3% vs 4.2%), and non-inferiority of BMV was not demonstrated.
ROSC was lower with BMV (28.4% vs 33.2%), but 28-day survival was nearly identical (5.4% vs 5.3%).
BMV had more regurgitation (15.2%) and airway failure (6.7%), while ETI had a high rate of recognised oesophageal intubation (10.2%).

outcomes_table.outcome: Favourable neurological outcome at day 28 (CPC 1-2) – ITT

outcomes_table.note: Composite procedural difficulty; open-label may influence reporting.
BMV group: rescue intubation in 146 patients (55 ventilation failure, 100 gastric regurgitation; not mutually exclusive).
Recognised and corrected. Also mainstem intubation 21/1030 (2.0%), dental injury 7/1030 (0.7%), accidental extubation 5/1030 (0.5%).

safety: BMV: regurgitation 156/1028 (15.2%), airway failure 69/1028 (6.7%); rescue intubation performed in 146 (55 ventilation failure, 100 regurgitation).
ETI: recognised oesophageal intubation 105/1030 (10.2%), mainstem intubation 21/1030 (2.0%), dental injury 7/1030 (0.7%), accidental extubation 5/1030 (0.5%).
Composite procedural difficulty higher with BMV (18.1% vs 13.4%, risk difference 4.7%, p=0.004).

domains.notes: Centre-stratified, permuted blocks, sealed opaque envelopes opened in field; adequate concealment.
Open-label delivery; primary outcome assessed by blinded investigator, reducing detection bias.
3/2043 excluded from ITT (2 DNR, 1 not in cardiac arrest). Per-protocol numbers differed (BMV 995, ETI 943) due to crossovers/deviations.
Substantial rescue intubation in BMV arm (146, 14.3%) and some crossover in ETI arm (14 received BMV initially); strategy separation diluted.
Well balanced: mean age 67.5 vs 68.7 years, male 67.1% vs 67.1%, bystander CPR 70.5% vs 72.7%, asystole 61.4% vs 60.9%, collapse-to-ALS time 15 min (IQR 10–23) in both groups.
CPC at 28 days, standard but coarse; blinded assessment; susceptible to post-resuscitation care variability.
Planned size achieved; low event rate widened confidence intervals; non-inferiority not demonstrated despite near-identical point estimates.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall internal validity moderate: randomisation and blinded outcome assessment are strengths, but open-label delivery, substantial rescue/crossover, and low event rate limit precision and interpretability.

domains.notes: Restricted to non-shockable OHCA with very low survival (4% favourable outcome); not applicable to shockable rhythms or higher-survival populations.
Physician-staffed EMS with high ETI skill; thresholds for BMV failure/rescue may differ in paramedic-led or resource-limited systems. Supraglottic devices not tested.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability moderate: most applicable to physician-led EMS treating predominately non-shockable OHCA, less so to other system configurations and patient populations.

strengths: Large, pragmatic, multicentre RCT with centre-stratified randomisation and allocation concealment.
Clinically meaningful primary endpoint assessed by a blinded investigator.
Prespecified non-inferiority framework with supportive per-protocol and modified ITT analyses.
Broad real-world prehospital cohort within a defined rhythm category.
limitations: Open-label design may introduce performance bias in intermediate outcomes (e.g., airway difficulty).
Restricted to non-shockable rhythms, yielding low event rate and limited applicability to shockable rhythms.
Frequent rescue intubation in BMV arm (14.3%) dilutes strategy separation.
Airway-related mechanisms (chest compression interruption, ventilation quality) not quantified.
Non-inferiority margin (1.0% absolute) proportionally large relative to ~4% event rate; interpretation sensitive to CI width.

critical_appraisal.summary: Despite randomisation and blinded outcome assessment, the trial did not establish non-inferiority of BMV vs ETI due to very low event rates and dilution from frequent crossover, but near-identical patient-centred outcomes suggest clinical equipoise.
weaknesses: Substantial rescue intubation reducing strategy separation
Restricted to non-shockable rhythms reducing generalisability

sections.authors_conclusion: In non-shockable OHCA, BMV did not meet non-inferiority criteria vs ETI; the nearly identical neurological outcomes and survival, together with differing safety trade-offs, support equipoise and the importance of matching airway strategy to system capabilities.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not abandon BMV or mandate ETI; outcomes are similar. BMV carries higher risk of regurgitation/airway failure, ETI carries risk of oesophageal intubation. Choose strategy based on provider skill, system resources, and scenario.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Non-traumatic OHCA with non-shockable rhythm, treated in physician-led or similarly skilled prehospital systems.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: ETI is superior to BMV for neurologic outcome in all OHCA patients; point estimates were nearly identical and the trial studied a low-survival subgroup.
implementation_caveats: If using BMV, ensure rapid response to regurgitation (suction, early consideration of definitive airway).
Emphasize rigorous ETI placement confirmation (waveform capnography) and preparedness for oesophageal intubation.
In paramedic-only systems, supraglottic devices may be an alternative intermediate strategy; they were not tested here.
The trial does not address airway strategy for shockable rhythms or patients with high predicted survival.

controversies.notes: With favourable outcome ~4%, a 1% absolute non-inferiority margin is proportionally large; result sensitive to small shifts and protocol deviations.
Rescue intubation in 146 BMV patients (14.3%) indicates pragmatic step-up practice but dilutes strategy separation and complicates attribution of downstream effects.
Physician-staffed ETI performance and BMV failure thresholds may not translate to paramedic systems, where supraglottic devices are often the default intermediate airway.

controversies.topic: Relationship to other pragmatic airway RCTs
controversies.notes: Two 2018 trials (AIRWAYS-22 and PART3) compared supraglottic devices with ETI and found no clear functional superiority, aligning with CAAM’s message that airway choice should be system-appropriate.

Resuscitation guidelines now emphasise choosing an airway strategy that minimises interruptions and matches provider competence; BMV and supraglottic airways are appropriate early strategies, ETI reserved for highly trained operators.

context_related_trials.relation: Compared i-gel supraglottic device vs ETI; no difference in neurological outcome but higher initial airway success with i-gel, highlighting safety trade-offs similar to CAAM.
Compared laryngeal tube vs ETI; no difference in 72-hour survival but better airway success with laryngeal tube, supporting the concept that intermediate airways are viable alternatives.

unresolved_questions: What are the quantitative effects of airway technique on chest compression interruption and ventilation quality during BMV vs ETI?
How would a BMV-first strategy perform in paramedic-only systems with different rescue thresholds and ETI success rates?
Does initial airway strategy interact with post-resuscitation care (e.g., TTM, early angiography) to affect neurological outcome?
Would BMV be non-inferior in a population with higher baseline survival (e.g., shockable rhythms) where complication rates might differ?
How should advanced airway timing and technique be incorporated into optimal CPR bundles for prolonged downtime or refractory arrest?
What is the role of supraglottic airways as a bridge between BMV and ETI in this population?

numbers_to_remember: Favourable neurological outcome at 28 days: 4.3% vs 4.2% (risk difference 0.11%)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In non-shockable OHCA, bag-mask ventilation is not inferior to endotracheal intubation for neurologic outcome—either strategy works similarly; choose based on skill and system, knowing BMV risks regurgitation and ETI risks misplacement.
